newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Oct 31.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Oct 31.

text.p: A parcel bomb police said was "designed to kill" exploded in the faces of two Wellington university students on Wednesday. Its failure to detonate properly saved their lives, police said. Page 1.

Labour and NZ First have been discussing costings for a coalition policy programme, with NZ First questioning the affordability of Labour's budget figures. NZ First leader Winston Peters argued in the election campaign that Labour's promises were unaffordable and is understood to have taken that argument into post-election talks this week. NZ First is understood to be concerned it should not appear as the less financially generous party in a coalition with Labour. It would prefer Labour to scale down its spending commitments without indicating NZ First has forced cutbacks. Page 1.

Quick action by a friend of Winston Peters saved the NZ First leader from being punched in the head by a former boxer at a Wellington cafe opening on Wednesday, witnesses said. Moments earlier, staff had broken up a heated row between Peters and a senior media executive. Page 1.
A senior British fraud investigator has endorsed the Serious Fraud Office's handling of the Winebox documents relating to Cook Islands tax haven deals. Page 2.

Tranz Rail wants to sell off $132 million of rolling stock and lease it back. A company spokeswoman would not comment on the proposal, listed in the company's annual report, saying details would be given in a few weeks. Page 2.

Tomato processer Cedenco was "plunged into uncertainty" by an insurance dispute only months after the company listed on the Stock Exchange, the Auckland High Court was told on Wednesday. The dispute arose over compensation claims for crops ruined by rain in late 1992 and early 1993. Cedenco is seeking $3.046 million for unpaid insurance claims. Page 13.

Business confidence fell "considerably" just before the election, according to the latest National Bank survey released on Thursday. However, businesses were still generally positive that conditions would improve in the next 12 months. There was some concern that the confidence was partly hinged on expected interest rate falls. A net 28 percent of those surveyed expected rates to fall. Page 13.

A higher inflation target for the Reserve Bank would, at best, mean a short term fall in interest rates but possibly lead to higher rates over time, according to a study by the National Bank. Page 13.
The TAB increased racing turnover to a record $921 million for the year to June 30, up $81 million on the previous year, chief executive George Hickton said on Wednesday. Page 13.

The Prime Minister was clearly annoyed on Wednesday at the non-appearance of Winston Peters at the coalition talks - just hours after the New Zealand First leader was asked to leave a Wellington restaurant party. Peters says the incident was regrettable but the no-show had nothing to do with the early morning party. Prime Minister Jim Bolger received only five minutes' notice that Peters would not show up to the 10 a.m. coalition talks with National on Wednesday.

New Zealand is in uncharted territory with its light-handed approach to regulation of the electricity industry, according to an American expert on the industry Leonard Kujawa. "I don't know anyone else who follows the approach of saying 'Everone be good boys'. It's sort of a chaplain's approach to regulation, which in the business world is a little different," said Kujawa, worldwide director, energy and telecommunications, with the international accounting firm Arthur Andersen.

A sharp fall in United States interest rates attracted attention away from New Zealand money markets on Wednesday. The United States 30-year bond interest rate dropped 16 points to 6.67 percent, cheered by a new batch of economic data. New Zealand and Australian bond markets followed the moves and the New Zealand 2006 bond interest rate dropped nine points to 7.26 percent.

Standard and Poor's has assigned a BBB minus corporate credit rating and A-3 short-term rating to Fernz Corporation. "Ratings on Fernz reflect a moderate financial risk profile, solid positions in several chemical commodity markets and a strong competitive position in its key regional fertiliser business," the ratings agency said.

Shareholders in newly floated National Mutual can still trade their shares despite not having received share certificates yet, according to general manager Ross McEwan. The company had made arrangements with the stock exchange.
